guides.title: Tea Tree as a Field Antiseptic
guides.summary: Tea tree preparations can support minor skin-cleaning routines in the field, but they do not replace proper first aid, wound irrigation, or medical treatment.
steps: Wash hands and irrigate the minor skin area with the cleanest water you have first.
Use only diluted, skin-safe tea tree preparation on small intact skin areas unless a clinician has told you otherwise.
Stop immediately if stinging, rash, or breathing symptoms appear.
Cover the area with a clean dressing and monitor for infection or worsening pain.
guides.notes: Do not use concentrated oils in eyes, deep wounds, large burns, or on infants. Seek medical care if infection, fever, spreading redness, or severe pain develops.

guides.title: Eucalyptus Field Uses
guides.summary: Eucalyptus is best treated as a comfort or hygiene aid in the field, not as a replacement for asthma care, infection treatment, or emergency airway management.
steps: Use eucalyptus only in low-intensity ways such as steam inhalation nearby or topical products already known to be safe for you.
Keep use well away from children, pets, eyes, and flames.
Stop if coughing, wheezing, rash, or dizziness worsens.
Return to standard first aid and prescribed medication plans first if someone is unwell.
guides.notes: Do not treat breathing distress, asthma attack, or serious infection with bush remedies alone. Call emergency services for severe breathing trouble.

guides.title: Lemon Myrtle and Paperbark Field Uses
guides.summary: Lemon myrtle and paperbark are best used as practical field materials for comfort, wrapping, and scent-based hygiene support when standard supplies are limited.
steps: Use clean paperbark as a temporary outer wrap only when you do not have a proper sterile dressing.
Keep any leaf or bark material away from deep wounds until the area is irrigated and covered properly.
Use lemon myrtle only in known-safe food or diluted wash contexts, not as an emergency medicine substitute.
Replace natural wraps with standard first-aid dressings as soon as possible.
guides.notes: Natural materials can carry dirt and irritation risk. Do not rely on them for serious wounds, burns, bites, or infections.

guides.title: Bush Tucker Medicinal Plant Basics
guides.summary: Native medicinal plants should be treated conservatively. Correct identification matters, and supportive use is safer than trying to improvise strong remedies in the field.
steps: Only use plants you can confidently identify from prior learning or a trusted reference.
Prefer supportive uses like known-safe teas, washes, or soothing compresses over strong ingestion or oils.
Test only tiny amounts first and stop if irritation or allergy symptoms appear.
Log what was used in case symptoms worsen and professional help is needed later.
guides.notes: Never guess plant identity in an emergency. Misidentification can be dangerous. Seek medical help for poisoning, bites, serious pain, or infection.

guides.title: Snake Bite Pressure Bandage Refresh
guides.summary: Pressure immobilisation is a specific first-aid skill used in Australia for certain venomous bites. RediM8 routes full snake-bite questions to the dedicated critical guide.
steps: Keep the person still and calm and call emergency services urgently.
Apply a firm broad pressure bandage over the bite area and continue up the limb.
Splint the limb and keep the person completely still until professional help arrives.
Do not wash the bite, cut the skin, suck venom, or use a tourniquet.
guides.notes: This is a refresher only. Use the full RediM8 snake-bite guide for the complete deterministic first-aid flow.
